name: The Betteleiche

location.address: At the crossing of the Rennstieg and the Hohe Strasse near Ihlefeld, Nationalpark Hainich, Thuringia

access: Free. Inside Nationalpark Hainich, reached by several waymarked hiking trails including the dedicated Betteleichenweg, plus the Waagebalkenweg, Hainichlandweg and Rennstieg long-distance trails. No ticket or booking needed, but it is a walk-in forest destination rather than a roadside stop.
transport: No rail or bus stop nearby; reached on foot from national park trailheads near Kammerforst or Weberstedt, typically 45 minutes to over an hour of walking depending on the trailhead. Not a public-transport day trip; visitors normally drive to a trailhead car park and walk in.
story:
Monks are said to have cut a hollow into this oak so that the alms would stay dry. From 1442 to 1525 a Franciscan mendicant house stood at nearby Ihlefeld, an annex of the St Catherine's monastery at Eisenach, and travellers crossing the forest left coins and prayer requests for the friars at the tree rather than at the door. The name stuck: Betteleiche, the begging oak.

What people walk in to see now is the shape. The trunk stands as two shells that fuse again about four metres up, a gateway you can step through, and centuries of weather have widened the gap. The tree is 13 metres tall, short for an oak of this weight, and about 5.9 metres round at a metre above the ground, though one summary puts it nearer 5.6. Sources agree on 600 to 800 years, and none of them cored it to find out.

It is the symbol of Nationalpark Hainich, with a waymarked trail named after it, the Betteleichenweg, and the Rennstieg and Hainichlandweg crossing at the same point. Reaching it means 45 minutes of walking or more from the nearest trailhead, in whatever the weather is doing. Which oak it is remains open: the sources say only Eiche, sessile or pedunculate unsettled. If you know, tell us.

name: The Hunneneiche

location.address: Schlossweg, 96190 Untermerzbach, Bavaria (western edge of the village, beside the Gasthaus Hunneneiche)

access: Free, open around the clock. Free-standing on a meadow at the edge of the village next to a restaurant of the same name (Gasthaus Hunneneiche), reachable without a detour from the B4 highway.
transport: Rural village with no rail station; nearest bus stops serve Untermerzbach itself. Realistically a car-accessible destination rather than a public-transport day trip from a city.
story:
Two sources disagree about this oak's age by nearly three centuries, and neither has given way. The Naturpark Hassberge, which lists it for visitors, says about 500 years. The dendrologist Rainer Lippert, who documents Bavaria's monumental oaks one specimen at a time, works from a recorded planting around 1700 give or take a hundred years, which puts the tree somewhere between 220 and 420. Both figures are published. Nobody has cored the trunk to close the gap.

What has been measured is less arguable. The trunk was 6.61 metres round in 2014 and climbs about ten metres as a near cylinder before it releases into limbs, which is why the oak reads as a column from the road. It stands 21 metres tall and is hollow inside, betrayed only by a few small openings.

It grows alone on a meadow at the western edge of Untermerzbach, on open ground off the Schlossweg, and has been a legally protected natural monument since 31 July 1963. The inn beside it took the tree's name rather than the other way round: the Gasthaus Hunneneiche is what most drivers coming off the B4 notice first, and this oak is the reason it is called that.

There is no gate, no ticket and no opening hour. The meadow is simply there, at any time of day or year.

name: Hueter des Feldes (the Rasierpinselbaum)
age_estimate: sources disagree, several hundred to over a thousand years

location.address: Beside the road to Nedensdorf, about 500m south of the junction near Gleussen, Bad Staffelstein, Landkreis Lichtenfels, Bavaria

access: Free, standing in open fields beside a public road, with a stone bench at its base for visitors. No ticket or restriction.
transport: Rural location near Bad Staffelstein; no rail or bus stop at the tree itself, reached by road. Not a public-transport day trip from a city.
story:
The 2003 feature film Luther put its young monk under this oak to shelter from a thunderstorm. It still stands where the camera found it, in open fields beside the road to Nedensdorf, with a stone bench at its back for whoever walks out.

Both of its nicknames describe the crown. Hueter des Feldes, guardian of the field. Rasierpinselbaum, shaving-brush tree, for the bristled shape that generations of pollarding left behind.

Its age depends entirely on who is asked, and the gap is enormous. Baumkunde's dendrology puts it at 300 to 500 years. German Wikipedia, the local press and the Bayreuth conservation authority all speak of more than a thousand, the authority phrasing it as a tree ready to die after roughly 1000 years. That is the real spread, and narrowing it would be an invention.

The condition matters before anyone travels. Fungal disease has been killing parts of the crown since about 2013, and the droughts of 2018 and 2019 pushed it further. The trunk is completely hollow, its walls as thin as 20 centimetres in places. One side is bare, the surviving leaves come smaller than they should, and the tree has stopped setting acorns. Bayreuth has decided against further preservation and is letting it go naturally. A visit in June 2026 still recorded it as vital, hollow, crown partly green. At 6.16 metres round in 2025 against 6.14 in 2011, it has essentially stopped growing.

name: The Kaiser-Lothar-Linde

location.address: On the meadow beside the Kaiserdom (Stiftskirche) collegiate church, Konigslutter am Elm, Lower Saxony
location.neighbourhood: Konigslutter am Elm town centre, beside the Kaiserdom

access: Free and publicly accessible (baumkunde.de states 'oeffentlich zugaenglich'), standing on open ground next to the Kaiserdom, a major visited monument in its own right.
transport: Konigslutter am Elm has its own railway station on the Braunschweig-Helmstedt line; the tree stands a short walk from the town centre beside the Kaiserdom.
story:
There is brickwork inside this lime. When tree surgeons treated the hollow trunk in 1975 they lined the cavity with masonry, fitted grilles over the openings and hung the crown from wire cables. That is ordinary veteran-tree care rather than a sign of a tree on its way out: the register still lists its health as vital.

The girth explains the effort. Baumkunde measured 13.32 metres round on 31 August 2021, against an older and rounder 12.50 that still circulates in print. Height is given as about 20 metres.

Legend hands the tree both a planter and a date: Emperor Lothar III, at the groundbreaking of the Kaiserdom beside it in 1135, which is where the name comes from and why people here say thousand-year linden. Dendrology puts it at 850 to 900 years, an estimate rather than a planting record, so the emperor stays a story.

What is documented is the work it did. This was a Gerichts- und Tanzlinde, the lime under which the court sat and the village danced, on the green beside one of Lower Saxony's great Romanesque churches. It has been under legal protection since 1956.

Konigslutter am Elm has its own station on the Braunschweig to Helmstedt line, and the tree stands a short walk away on open ground, free, with a cathedral for a neighbour.

name: The Fuenffingerlinde

location.address: A clearing in the Riesewohld forest, about 500m south of Quellental and the A23 motorway, near Odderade, Kreis Dithmarschen, Schleswig-Holstein
location.neighbourhood: Riesewohld forest, near Odderade and Albersdorf

access: Free, open year-round. Benches are placed around the tree and marked hiking trails lead to the clearing in the Riesewohld forest.
transport: Rural forest location a few minutes' drive from Albersdorf; no rail or bus stop at the site itself. Reached on foot from a forest car park, not a public-transport day trip.
story:
Five stems, one tree, and the shape of an open hand. The Fuenffingerlinde grew its trunks together over the centuries into a form people read as a palm with fingers, one lower branch pushed forward as the thumb, and it has been a protected natural monument since 1938 on the strength of that shape rather than its size.

The story attached to it is a hanging. A wanderer was executed nearby for something he had not done, and the hand in the tree is said to stand for his innocence, so that nobody could tidy the case away. That is regional legend rather than record, and it is what brings most people down the track.

The measurements are modest and the growth curve is honest. Just under 4 metres round in 1932, 4.90 metres when baumkunde measured it on 21 June 2020: 90 centimetres in 88 years. The estimate is 250 to 300 years, young beside the court limes of central Germany and no less odd to stand beneath.

It grows in a clearing in the Riesewohld forest near Odderade, with benches set around it and marked hiking trails leading in. The same 2020 survey recorded its health as vital. Free, open all year, a few minutes' drive from Albersdorf and then a walk from the forest car park.

name: The Riesenlinde zu Heede (Giant Lime of Heede)

location.address: At the village entrance to Heede, off a side lane (Pinnincksallee) from the Hauptstrasse, Landkreis Emsland, Lower Saxony

access: Free and open, standing at the village entrance and used as the village's traditional gathering point for religious services, processions and ceremonies.
transport: Rural Emsland village with no rail station; nearest town with rail access is Papenburg, roughly 20-25 minutes by car. Not a public-transport day trip.
story:
This is widely reported as the thickest lime tree in Europe, and the two published figures for its waist sit nearly two metres apart. German Wikipedia says 15.39 metres. The Nationalerbe-Baeume programme, measuring in December 2018 at 1.30 metres above the ground, gives about 17.50. Take either one and there is still nothing comparable in a village this size.

Heede put the tree on its coat of arms. It stands at the entrance to the place, off a side lane from the Hauptstrasse, and remains the point where processions form and open-air services are held, which is the work a village lime has always done here.

People call it the thousand-year lime. No expert will sign that off, and the sourced estimate is 600 to 800 years. The nickname is affection rather than dendrology.

Its formal status is Nationalerbe-Baum, the federal designation reserved for Germany's most outstanding individual trees, which buys it support structures and continuous care. That programme's own documentation, from 2019 and 2020 with the last noted maintenance visit in March 2020, called the tree still completely healthy. Height is put at 20 metres, or roughly 24 by estimate.

Heede has no station. Papenburg, the nearest town on the railway, is 20 to 25 minutes away by car. At the tree itself there is no gate, no ticket and no hour.

name: The Collmer Linde

location.address: Kirchanger am Dorfplatz/Kirchberg, directly beside the small Romanesque church in Collm, Gemeinde Wermsdorf, Landkreis Nordsachsen

access: Free and open, standing on the churchyard green (Kirchanger) beside the village church at the centre of Collm, a public village square.
transport: Rural Saxon village; nearest larger town is Oschatz. No rail station at Collm itself. Not a public-transport day trip from a city.
story:
Justice for the Meissen region was handed down under this lime. The green beside the small Romanesque church at Collm was in all probability the Dingplatz, the assembly site where the court sat, more than 800 years ago, and the tree on it is the tree that was there.

Saxony calls it the oldest linden in the state. People here have said a thousand years for the better part of a century, but a forestry botanist's assessment puts the real figure nearer 800, so the honest band is 700 to 900 and the millennium stays a habit rather than a measurement.

Arborists went over it properly in May 2022. Their inspection recorded vigorous secondary stems, documented new growth and a population of long-eared bats living in it, and what came out of it was a plan for future crown maintenance rather than removal. That October the trunk measured 11.05 metres round at 1.3 metres, and on 22 October 2022 the tree was declared a Nationalerbe-Baum, one of the federal register of Germany's most outstanding specimens.

Its recorded height wanders between 15 and 32 metres depending on the year, which is what repeated crown work does to a number rather than a sign anybody miscounted. It stands about 25 metres now.

The tree is on the churchyard green at the centre of the village, on a public square, free and open.

name: The Kaiserlinde at Schloss Burg

location.address: Beside the Seilbahn Burg cable car's mountain station, Schlossplatz, Schloss Burg, Solingen, North Rhine-Westphalia
location.neighbourhood: Schloss Burg an der Wupper, Solingen

access: Free, accessible at any time (naturparkbergischesland.de: 'kostenfrei / jederzeit zugaenglich'), standing in the open grounds around Schloss Burg next to the cable car's mountain station, outside the paid castle museum itself.
transport: Reached by the Seilbahn Burg cable car from the Wupper valley, or on foot; Solingen and the Schloss Burg area are served by local bus routes from Solingen Hbf.
story:
Members of a religious order pruned this lime into a room. Over generations they trained its branches into a living bower with a hut-like platform inside, reached by a ladder, and climbed up there to pray the breviary out of everyone's way. The tree stood at the centre of the Catholic rectory garden at Schloss Burg, which was a far larger garden then than the open ground it occupies now.

The shaping has consequences. Nobody publishes a girth for it, because there is no ordinary trunk to put a tape around: German Wikipedia states outright that the circumference cannot be measured meaningfully on a form this irregular. Age is given as roughly 250 years, inside a band of 200 to 300.

Which lime it is has not been settled either. German Wikipedia calls it a Tilia x europaea 'Pallida'. The Naturpark Bergisches Land calls it a Tilia cordata. We publish it as a lime and leave the species open; if you can settle it, tell us.

Since 1952 the tree has belonged to the cable car company. It stands beside the mountain station of the Seilbahn Burg, outside the ticketed part of the castle, and Solingen coordinates care work on it roughly every three years. It is natural monument number 51 in the city's 2007 ordinance. Free, at any hour, and you can arrive by cable car.
